o: Range to the far edge, bearing to the centre
Range to the centre, bearing to one end
Range and bearing both to the left end
why: Range is sharp at the echo’s leading edge; the beam width smears bearing both ways, so take the centre of a point target.

a: Tune, then raise the gain to a faint speckle
o: Turn the sea clutter control to maximum
Turn the rain clutter control up full
Lower the gain further to keep it clean
why: A clean screen usually means too little gain or poor tuning: tune for the strongest echoes, then gain up to a light background.

a: The sea clutter control has wiped out her echo
o: Yachts never show on radar in a seaway
She is inside the radar’s minimum range
Her AIS is wrong — trust the radar
why: Sea clutter (STC) cuts close-range gain; at maximum it removes small echoes too. Set it to leave a little clutter showing.

a: Use the rain control to break up the rain and find her
o: Raise the gain until the patch is solid
Turn up the sea clutter control instead
Rely on the AIS — radar cannot see in rain
why: The rain control (FTC) keeps only the leading edges of echoes, thinning the rain so a ship’s echo inside it can stand out.

o: Rely on the radar — 8° is too narrow to matter
Turn up the gain to see through the mast
Use a longer range scale to see past it
why: A ship can hide in a blind sector for many minutes; alter 10–15° from time to time and keep a visual lookout ahead.

A second small reflector beside the first
Your own radar left on transmit

o: To the far end of the racon paint
To the middle of the racon paint
To the end of the dash, less a mile
why: The racon paint starts just beyond the beacon’s own echo: its near end gives the range, the line’s direction the bearing.

About 190°T at 14 kn

o: They are right — she will cross a mile ahead

Only once the bearing is steady for 20 min

In the basin, where she has room to turn
Wherever the helmsman starts to feel unsure
why: With the swell from astern a 24 m yacht is committed once past the heads; decide go or no-go where you can still turn and stand off.

fig.title: Entry plan — narrow harbour, 0300
lines: Entrance 40 m wide; inner basin 90 m across
Swell from astern, 1.5 m
Your yacht 24 m; turning circle about 60 m
The plan needs an abort point

q: You reach the reporting point and call VTS, as the pilot book asks. What does your report give?
a: Name, position, intentions and ETA at the berth
o: Only your name, and that you will keep clear
Your crew list and last port, as for customs
Nothing until VTS asks you for details
why: VTS fits you into its traffic picture: who you are, where, where bound and when. Then keep watch on its channel.

fig.title: Calling VTS at point BRAVO
lines: Your yacht: 23 m, inbound at night
Pilot book: report at BRAVO on ch 12
Then keep watch on ch 12 to the berth

q: Inbound in fog, you hear VTS give this. What do you do with it?
a: Find her on radar and plot her as any other ship
o: Hold your course — VTS will keep you apart
Ask VTS to give you a course to steer
Ignore it — VTS messages are for ships
why: Traffic information is not traffic control: it tells you she is coming. The lookout, the plot and the Rules stay with you.

fig.title: VTS, 0420, fog
lines: "Aurora leaving berth 4, outbound"
"This is traffic information only"
You: inbound, 1.5 M from the entrance
Radar on; visibility 0.2 M

q: Your 24 m yacht must turn onto the leading line tonight. How far short of the point where the two tracks meet do you put the wheel over?
a: About 140 m
o: About 200 m
About 550 m
About 110 m
why: Wheel-over distance = radius × tan(half the turn) = 200 × tan 35° = 140 m before the tracks meet.

fig.title: Night entry — onto the leading line
lines: Turn 70° to starboard onto the line
Turning radius at your helm angle: 200 m
Ignore her delay in answering the helm

q: You are finishing the contingencies of your plan for a 140 M crossing. What does its medical line list?
a: Ports with a hospital on each stage, and the radio medical route
o: The crew’s next of kin and their home phones
Only the contents of the first-aid kit
The nearest airports for flying crew home
why: A casualty 100 M out needs a plan: which ports on each stage have a hospital, and how to reach radio medical advice via the MRCC.

fig.title: Passage plan — contingencies
lines: Ports of refuge: listed for each stage
Weather: plan B for a gale
Medical: ?

q: A crew member is hurt halfway across, as on the card. Which way gets him to a hospital soonest?
a: Port B — in about 0653, the hospital at the port
o: Port A — the nearest, in about 0700
Home — back alongside by about 0847
On to the destination — about 0900
why: B: 50 ÷ 8.5 = 5.9 h → 0653, hospital there. A is in at 0700 but 2 h from one (0900); home 0847; on, 0900.

fig.title: 0100, 70 M out of 130: crew member hurt
lines: Radio medical: ashore to a hospital, soon
A: 30 M upwind at 5 kn; hospital 2 h by road
B: 50 M on a reach, 8.5 kn; hospital there
Home 70 M at 9 kn; destination 60 M at 7.5 kn

q: Your night orders set the fixing routine as on the card. When does the watch change to 6-minute fixes?
why: Six-minute fixes start 3 M from the bank: 10.5 − 3 = 7.5 M to run at 10 kn = 45 min after 0215 → 0300.

fig.title: Night orders — fixing
lines: Offshore: a fix every 30 min
Within 3 M of any danger: every 6 min
0215: 10.5 M from the bank, 10 kn, closing

q: Your 0300 fix lands well away from the EP, as on the card. What does your monitoring routine say now?
a: Find the cause, and fix more often until it is clear
o: Accept the fix and keep to the 30-minute routine
Ignore it — one odd fix is just an error
Steer back to where the EP put you
why: A 1.5 M jump in 30 min means a stream, a sensor or the plot is wrong; tighten the routine until you know which.

fig.title: 0300 — the fix and the plan
lines: 0230 fix on the track; 0300 EP on the track
0300 radar fix: 1.5 M east of the EP
Orders: a fix every 30 min offshore

q: You fly home tonight, and a relief skipper takes the yacht on, as on the card. What do you hand over first?
a: The plan and its changes, the defects and the crew
o: The keys, the ship’s papers and the fuel receipts
The plotter route — it holds all he needs
Nothing formal — he can read the log
why: The new skipper takes on the plan: what has changed, what is broken and who is fit for what. Papers and keys come after.

fig.title: Halfway port — you leave tonight
lines: Relief skipper joins at 1800
Sails at 0600 for the second 120 M leg
Watermaker weak; one crew new to nights

q: Your night route crosses the traffic lanes in the conditions on the card. How do you plan the crossing?
a: Motor-sail across at a steady speed and heading
o: Sail across slowly — a sailing yacht stands on
Wait in the separation zone for more wind
Sail along the lane until the wind fills in
why: At 3 kn on a wandering heading you spend 3 h in the lanes and confuse the ships; motor-sail for a steady heading and speed.

fig.title: Crossing the lanes, 2300
lines: 24 m ketch; the lanes 9 M across in all
Wind light and fickle, 4–8 kn
Under sail alone: 3–5 kn, heading wanders

q: Checking tonight’s route, you find WP4 here. What do you do?
a: Move it clear of the point where the ships turn
o: Keep it — ships keep clear of a yacht there
Keep it, and cross the point at full speed
Keep it, and call each ship on VHF
why: Ships converge and alter at the same point off a cape; a yacht turning there meets them all, mid-turn. Put WP4 clear of their routes.

fig.note: Ship routes from the routeing guide

q: It is the second afternoon at sea, as on the card. What do you do now to be ready for the landfall?
a: Send half the crew to sleep now, by turns
o: Keep everyone up — the landfall needs all hands
Give everyone coffee at 0300, before you close
Let them rest once the landfall is made
why: Rest is part of the plan: crew who sleep this afternoon and evening are fresh at 0400; coffee at 0300 does not undo 20 hours awake.

fig.title: 1500, the second day
lines: Landfall on a rocky coast at about 0400
Crew of five, all short of sleep
Two watches since yesterday 0800

q: You check the fuel before the run, as on the card. Which figure does your fuel plan use?
a: The dip — half, so you take on fuel first
o: The gauge — it is the newer reading
The mean of the two, about five-eighths
The gauge — a dip is spoilt by heel
why: A gauge sender sticks and drifts; the dip measures the fuel. Half is less than your plan needs, so fill up before you go.

fig.title: Before the 130 M run
lines: Fuel gauge: three-quarters
Dipstick in the tank: half
Plan needs five-eighths, reserve included

q: It is the morning of departure, as on the card. What is left to do before you slip?
a: Check the new forecast against the plan, then brief the crew
o: Nothing — the plan was finished last night
Draw the whole route again on the chart
Let the crew vote on whether to go
why: Execution: confirm the plan still fits the latest forecast and the boat, decide, then brief everyone on the plan, watches and plan B.

fig.title: Departure morning, 0600
lines: Plan made and checked last night
The 0520 forecast is in
Crew of six aboard

q: You take the motor yacht across ahead of the wind on the card. When do you expect to arrive?
a: About 1512
o: About 1445
About 2000
About 1646
why: 0600–1400 at 16 kn = 128 M; the last 12 M at 10 kn take 1 h 12 min → 1512, before the 1700 limit.

fig.title: Motor yacht, 140 M, leaving 0600
lines: 16 kn in calm water
From 1400: NE 6 on the nose; 10 kn at best
Your rule: in before 1700, when F7 arrives

q: You are setting up the night watches on your motor yacht, as on the card. What do you add for the lone watchkeeper?
a: A watch alarm that must be reset every few minutes
o: A radar guard zone to stand in for the lookout
Longer watches, so there are fewer handovers
The autopilot’s off-course alarm, nothing more
why: Alone at night with the autopilot steering, a watchkeeper can doze off unseen; an alarm that sounds unless reset catches it early.

fig.title: Night watch, 24 m motor yacht
lines: One watchkeeper on the flybridge
Autopilot steering, 2200–0600
Watches of two hours each

q: You plot this echo on the night watch. If neither of you alters, when does she reach you?
a: About 0248
o: About 0236
About 0257
About 0234
why: Steady bearing, CPA nil: 2.0 M closed in 12 min = 10 kn, so the 6.0 M left take 36 min from 0212 → 0248.

q: Two echoes close on you at once. Which is the more urgent, and when is her CPA?
a: B — CPA 0.3 M at about 0318
o: A — CPA nil at about 0342
B — CPA 0.3 M at about 0312
A — CPA nil at about 0336
why: A: steady bearing, nil CPA, but 36 min off (0342). B passes 0.3 M off in 12 min (0318): deal with B first, without closing A.

fig.title: Radar plot, own ship 000°T 10 kn
lines: Relative-motion display, north-up

q: You alter now to starboard for the CPA your orders ask. To what course do you alter?
a: About 046°T
o: About 024°T
About 028°T
About 314°T
why: From 040°, 5.0 M lay the line tangent to the 2 M ring (23.6° off); with her vector 261°, 9.8 kn the triangle gives 046°T.
ref: Radar plotting — the alteration for a CPA

fig.title: Radar plot, own ship 000°T 10 kn
lines: 0130  target 040°T, 8.0 M
0142  target 040°T, 5.0 M
Alter at 0142 to starboard, still 10 kn
Orders: a CPA of at least 2 M

q: Rather than turn, you slow down as on the card. What CPA does the new plot give?
a: About 2.4 M
o: Nil, as before
About 4.2 M
About 1.6 M
why: Her true vector 300°, 12 kn minus your 6 kn north gives relative motion 270°: from 060°, 4.8 M she passes 2.4 M ahead.

fig.title: Radar plot, own ship 000°T 12 kn
lines: 0400  target 060°T, 6.0 M
0406  target 060°T, 4.8 M
At 0406 you slow to 6 kn (take it as at once)

q: The third plot of this echo falls off the line of the first two. What CPA does she now give?
a: CPA 2.1 M at 0525
o: CPA nil at 0523
CPA 1.3 M at 0526
CPA 2.1 M at 0519
why: The bend at 0506 shows she has altered: plot afresh from 0506 and 0512 only. That line passes 2.1 M off, CPA at 0525.
ref: Radar plotting — a target that alters

q: Your route crosses a fast-ferry route tonight. At what range must the radar first show a ferry to give the warning your orders ask?
why: Relative speed = her 225°, 30 kn less your 000°, 12 kn = 39.4 kn; × 20 min = 13.1 M — beyond 12 M, so watch on the 24 M scale.

fig.title: Night orders, ferry route ahead
lines: Fast ferries: 30 kn, heading 225°T
Own ship 000°T, 12 kn
Orders: 20 min warning of any ferry
Radar scales: 3, 6, 12, 24 M

q: You hand over the radar watch for the night, as on the card. Which range scales does the watch use?
a: A long one for early warning, a short one for small craft
o: The 24 M scale only, for the earliest warning
The 3 M scale only, for the finest detail
Whichever scale shows the most echoes
why: Long scales give early warning of ships; small craft and buoys show only on a short scale. Switch between them on every look.

fig.title: Radar watch, 80 M offshore, night
lines: Sea state 3, a few showers
Ships and fishing boats about

q: This yacht’s echo appears 2 M off, and the guard zone never sounded. Why not?
a: Her echo first showed inside the zone’s inner edge
o: A guard zone works only on AIS targets
The zone filters out echoes as small as hers
The alarm waits until an echo has stayed 5 min
why: A small echo may first paint at 2–3 M; a ring from 6 M out never sees it. A guard zone helps the lookout, it does not replace one.

q: You are closing the coast at night in heavy rain, and the radar shows this. Why is there nothing behind the squall?
a: The rain soaks up the pulse, so echoes beyond it fade
o: Nothing is there — the coast has a gap
The rain control wipes out all echoes behind it
X-band sees through rain; the coast there is low
why: Heavy rain absorbs and scatters X-band energy, so targets beyond a squall fade or vanish. Slow down and look round its side.

fig.title: Radar, 0200, heavy rain ahead
lines: Squall 2–4 M ahead; rain control set
Coast at 9 M paints either side of it
Behind the squall: no coast, no echoes

q: You set a parallel index line to pass the cape, as on the card. Which way do you draw the line?
a: Parallel to the ground track, 045°T
o: Parallel to the heading, 033°T
Parallel to the cape’s coastline
Along the bearing of the cape now
why: A fixed echo moves across the screen opposite to your motion over the ground, so the index line runs parallel to the track, not the heading.
ref: Radar — parallel indexing with a stream

fig.title: Parallel index past the cape
lines: Planned track over the ground 045°T
Stream on the beam: heading 033°T holds it
Radar north-up, stabilised
Pass the cape 1.5 M off to port

q: A ship passes close and the radar paints this arc around her. What is it?
a: Side lobes from her strong echo, not real targets
o: A fleet of small craft around her
Her wake and the broken sea behind her
Second-trace echoes from far off
why: A big echo close by returns energy through the scanner’s side lobes, painting an arc at her range. Turn the gain or sea clutter down a touch.

q: You are tracking a ship on MARPA when this happens. What is the likely cause?
a: The tracker has jumped to the fishing boat’s echo
o: Ship A has slowed and turned towards you
The MARPA has found her real CPA at last
The fishing boat’s AIS has been fed into it
why: When two echoes pass close, MARPA may swap them and its data jump. Re-acquire both and check each by compass bearing and by eye.

fig.title: MARPA, 0330
lines: Acquired: ship A, CPA 1.8 M, 14 kn
Her echo passes close to a fishing boat
Now: vector swings, CPA 0.2 M, 3 kn

q: You switch the radar to true trails, as on the card. What do you make of the echo with no trail?
a: It is stopped — a buoy or a ship at anchor
o: It is on your course and at your speed
It is a false echo — real ones leave trails
It is closing you head-on at speed
why: Ground-stabilised true trails show movement over the ground, so no trail means stopped. In relative trails, an echo keeping pace with you has none.

fig.title: Radar, true trails (ground-stabilised)
lines: Ships’ echoes: trails behind each one
One echo 3 M ahead: no trail at all
Your speed 9 kn

q: In a strong cross-stream the ARPA and the ship’s lights disagree, as on the card. Why?
a: The vector shows her track over the ground, not her heading
o: Her lights are wrong — trust the vector
The ARPA has lost her and is guessing
Her navigation lights are set for a tow
why: In a cross-stream a ship crabs: ground-stabilised vectors show her course over the ground, her lights her heading. Sea-stabilise to judge aspect.

fig.title: 0215, strong tidal stream across
lines: ARPA vectors ground-stabilised (GNSS)
Ship ahead, steady 10 min: vector crossing
Her lights: masthead lights in line, red
and green both showing

q: The AIS shows a tanker 28 M away, but the radar shows nothing on her bearing. Why?
a: She is beyond your radar horizon; her AIS reaches further
o: Her AIS is false — trust the empty radar
The radar needs a 48 M scale to show her
Large ships paint only inside 12 M
why: Radar sees to its horizon: about 2.2 × (√8 + √30) ≈ 18 M to her bridge, while VHF from her high aerial carries further. Expect her echo later.

fig.title: 0100, AIS and radar
lines: AIS: tanker 28 M off, closing
Radar on 24 M: no echo on her bearing
Your scanner 8 m up; her bridge about 30 m

q: The radar and the AIS tell you different things about this ship, as on the card. Which do you believe?
a: The plot and her lights — the status is typed in by hand
o: The AIS status — she is moored, so ignore her
Neither — call her and wait for a reply
The AIS SOG alone — she is only drifting
why: Navigational status is set by her crew and often left wrong; her SOG, the plot and her lights say she is under way. Act on the risk.
ref: AIS — what it shows and what it does not

fig.title: 0330, radar and AIS
lines: AIS: cargo ship, status "moored", SOG 11.8 kn
Radar: her echo closing, bearing steady
Lights: masthead, sidelight, no anchor light

q: The radar shows two echoes in step, but the AIS shows one vessel, as on the card. What is the second echo?
a: Her tow — and you keep clear of the gap between them
o: A yacht in her wake — pass between the two
A false echo from the tug’s own hull
A second-trace echo from far astern
why: A tow often sends no AIS of its own. Two echoes in step with one AIS: treat it as a tow and never pass between them.

fig.title: 0130, radar and AIS
lines: AIS: tug "Hercules", 6 kn
Radar: her echo, and another 0.4 M astern
Second echo: same course and speed, no AIS

q: GNSS is lost mid-crossing, as on the card. What still works as before?
a: Radar, compass, log and sounder; the pilot on compass
o: Everything but the plotter’s position
The AIS and DSC, with fixes of their own
The autopilot, still steering the route
why: Without GNSS the AIS sends no position, DSC alerts carry none and track mode stops. Radar, compass, log and sounder carry on: DR and radar.
ref: GNSS — failure and what is left

fig.title: 0130, 60 M from landfall: GNSS lost
lines: Plotter: "no position fix"
Fitted: radar, fluxgate, log, sounder,
AIS, DSC VHF, autopilot in track mode

q: The GNSS fails on passage at night, as on the card. What do you do first?
a: Write down the last fix and time, and start a DR
o: Restart the plotter until it finds a fix
Head for the nearest land to get a fix
Wait — the satellites will soon come back
why: The last good fix with its time and log reading starts your DR; write it down before it scrolls off a screen.

fig.title: 0130: GNSS lost
lines: Last good fix 0100, log 406.2
Course steered 095°T

q: Approaching the strait, you find this. What do you trust?
a: The radar ranges — the GNSS may be spoofed
o: The GNSS — an HDOP of 0.8 shows it is sound
The mean of the two positions
The GNSS, after retuning the radar
why: Spoofing gives a smooth, confident and false fix with a good HDOP. Radar ranges and depths are independent: trust them, and report it.

fig.title: 0400, approaching the strait
lines: GNSS: steady fix, HDOP 0.8, SOG 9 kn
Radar ranges put you 2.5 M north of it
Two ships on AIS show inland, at an airport

q: The autopilot’s off-course alarm keeps sounding, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Reef or ease the main to take off the weather helm
o: Turn the autopilot’s gain up to its maximum
Widen the off-course alarm to 30°
Switch to wind mode to follow the gusts
why: No pilot beats the weather helm of an over-pressed yacht; balance her — reef, ease the main — and it will steer again.

fig.title: 0230, off-course alarm
lines: Autopilot on compass, close reach, F6
Heading swings 25° up in each gust
Full main, no reef; rudder hard over

q: At speed on the flybridge, the autopilot alarm shows this. What do you do first?
a: Take the helm in hand steering and slow down
o: Reset the autopilot and engage it again
Look up the fault code in the manual
Call the skipper, and wait at the helm
why: A drive fault can leave the rudder over at 18 kn: take hand steering at once and slow down, then look for the fault.

fig.title: Flybridge, 0100, 18 kn
lines: Autopilot alarm: "DRIVE FAULT"
Rudder angle shows hard over to port

q: Far offshore at night the sounder shows this. What do you make of it?
a: False echoes — fish, a layer in the water, or wake
o: An uncharted shoal — stop and sound around it
A seamount: the chart datum must be wrong
The sounder is right; the chart is out of date
why: Beyond its range a sounder can show fish, plankton layers or wake as depths; jumpy readings in 2,000 m are not a shoal.

fig.title: 0300, 70 M offshore
lines: Chart: 2,000 m of water here
Sounder: 14 m, then 22 m, then nothing
No shoal on the chart or in the Notices

q: Your log is out of action, so you work the plot from the GNSS, as on the card. How do you find the next hour’s position?
a: From COG and SOG alone — they hold the stream already
o: From COG and SOG, then apply the atlas stream
From heading and SOG, then apply the stream
Wait — with the log at 0.0 you have no plot
why: GNSS COG and SOG are over the ground, so the stream is in them. Laying the atlas stream on top counts it twice.

fig.title: Log out of action
lines: Paddlewheel fouled by weed: reads 0.0 kn
Using GNSS: COG 112°T, SOG 7.4 kn
Tidal atlas: stream 040°T, 1.2 kn

q: The log has failed, so you time a chip of wood along the deck. What is your speed through the water?
o: 5.5 kn
why: 22 m ÷ 4.0 s = 5.5 m/s; × 3,600 ÷ 1,852 = 10.7 kn through the water.

fig.title: Log fouled — checking the speed
lines: Marks on deck 22 m apart, bow to stern
The chip passes from mark to mark in 4.0 s

q: On the approach the radar overlay sits off the chart, as on the card. What do you navigate by?
a: Radar ranges — the plotter’s position may be off
o: The overlay — the radar is 0.3 M out
The charted coastline — echoes always lie off it
The mean of the chart and the echoes
why: A steady, uniform offset means the plotter’s position (the GNSS or the chart datum) is wrong, not the radar. Fix by radar ranges near the coast.
ref: Radar and the plotter — overlay offset

fig.title: Radar overlay on the plotter
lines: Coast echo 0.3 M east of the charted coast
The same offset all round, steady
Radar ranges to the cliffs agree together

q: The plotter shows this alarm, but the radar shows no line of dots on that bearing. Why not?
a: An AIS-SART sends AIS only — there is no radar reply
o: On test the dots are switched off
Your radar gain is too low to show them
The survivors are below the radar horizon
why: An AIS-SART (MMSI 970) reports its GNSS position by AIS; only a radar SART paints dots. Head for the AIS position and alert the MRCC.

fig.title: Plotter, 0510
lines: "SART ACTIVE", MMSI 970123456
Bearing 075°T, 6.5 M
Radar on 12 M: no line of dots there

q: The plotter sounds an alarm for this AIS target. What do you do?
a: Note it in the log — someone is testing a SART
o: Head for it and send a MAYDAY RELAY
Alert the MRCC — a liferaft is out
Switch the AIS alarms off for the day
why: An AIS-SART on test sends "SART TEST"; in distress it sends "SART ACTIVE". Log it and carry on; act at once on ACTIVE.

fig.title: Plotter alarm, 1015
lines: AIS target: MMSI 970111222
Text: "SART TEST"
4 M on the port beam

q: You are fitting out for a 150 M crossing, as on the card. Which backup do you add?
a: A handheld GNSS and VHF on their own batteries
o: A second plotter on the same network
A spare display for the main plotter
A larger house battery bank
why: A backup is a backup only if it shares nothing: its own aerial, power and screen. A second plotter on the same network fails with it.
ref: Integrated electronics — single point of failure

fig.title: Fit-out for a 150 M crossing
lines: All navigation on one NMEA 2000 network
One battery bank, one GNSS antenna

q: The GNSS fails 45 M from a low coast, as on the card. How do you plan the landfall now?
a: Aim off to one side, so you know which way to turn
o: Steer straight at the harbour on the DR
Wait offshore until the GNSS comes back
Follow a ship’s AIS track towards the coast
why: After 45 M of DR the error may lie either side. Aim off on purpose; at the coast the radar, sounder and light tell you to turn one way.

fig.title: GNSS lost, 0130 — 45 M to the landfall
lines: Harbour on a low coast; streams uncertain
Light on the point 3 M W of it: Fl(2) 10s 20M
Radar, sounder and DR all good
